script.opening: "Thanks doctor. So my liver blood test came back a bit high, which baffled me — I barely touch alcohol, maybe a couple of beers at the weekend. So surely it can't be a liver thing? I figured it's just one of those blips, or maybe a paracetamol I took. Can you just reassure me it's nothing and we move on? I haven't got a drink problem, if that's what you're thinking."

facts.text: If asked: tired for a few months; the nurse did bloods twice and the liver test was up both times.
"Two bottles of beer on a Saturday, that's it" — about 4 units a week. Never more. No morning drinking.
Tired. No yellowing, no itching, no tummy swelling, no vomiting blood, no black stools. Snores; wife says you sometimes stop breathing.
Desk job, long hours, takeaways three or four times a week, sugary drinks, no exercise since your knee went. Weight has crept up "about three stone in ten years".
None regularly. Paracetamol occasionally — "two tablets, once or twice a month". No supplements or herbal remedies. No allergies.
Dad had type 2 diabetes and a heart attack at 58.
49, accountant, married with two teenagers. Never smoked. No drug use, no tattoos.

Your dad's heart attack: "I'm nine years off his age." You have also felt judged about your weight before by a doctor and are braced for a lecture. Say these only if asked what worries you or about your family.

Defensive at first, keen to close it down. If the doctor implies you drink, bristle: "I told you, I barely drink." If they explain it is a fatty liver linked to weight, sugar and blood pressure — not drink — you are surprised and become engaged: "So what do I actually need to do?" Respond badly to a lecture, well to a practical, respectful plan.

ice.ideas: "It's a blip — or the odd paracetamol. It can't be my liver if I barely drink."
ice.concerns: Being judged. Underneath (only if asked): your dad's heart attack.
ice.expectations: "Reassure me it's nothing and we move on." You will engage with a plan if it is explained without blame.

cues: "I haven't got a drink problem, if that's what you're thinking." — say in the opening.
"My dad had diabetes too." — say if family history or sugar is mentioned.
"I know, I know — the weight." — say defensively when lifestyle comes up.

checkpoints.text: Corrects the misconception and explains NAFLD: a mildly raised ALT with central obesity, pre-diabetes and raised triglycerides (and a negative viral/autoimmune/iron screen, minimal alcohol) is non-alcoholic fatty liver disease — metabolic, NOT alcohol — so "I barely drink" does not exclude a liver cause

Assesses FIBROSIS RISK rather than just re-checking the ALT or reassuring: calculates a non-invasive fibrosis score (e.g. FIB-4, BSG/BASL 2018) and/or arranges an ELF test per NICE NG49 (advanced fibrosis if 10.51 or above) and a liver ultrasound — recognising that the ALT level does NOT reflect fibrosis severity

Manages the WHOLE metabolic/CVD picture: weight/lifestyle (the key treatment — even modest weight loss reduces liver fat), blood pressure (142/90), the pre-diabetes (HbA1c 44), lipids/triglycerides and overall cardiovascular risk — recognising NAFLD as a metabolic-syndrome/CVD-risk marker
Excludes the other causes appropriately (already largely done: viral hepatitis, autoimmune, haemochromatosis/iron, drugs) and confirms alcohol intake honestly, without making it the focus

Frames management POSITIVELY and hopefully: NAFLD is common and largely reversible with the same changes that improve weight, BP, sugar and heart risk — a fixable warning, not a verdict — and refers to hepatology if significant fibrosis is found
Hears the defensiveness and the avoidance, reframes without blame or a "drink problem" implication, and engages him in the metabolic conversation rather than colluding with "it’s nothing"
Addresses the fear that "liver" means something sinister with honest, proportionate reassurance balanced against the need to assess fibrosis

Safety-nets and follows up: the fibrosis assessment (FIB-4/ELF/ultrasound) and re-check plan, weight/BP/glucose/lipid management and review, hepatology referral if fibrosis, and a follow-up that treats the metabolic picture — not a one-off reassurance

worked.txt: "I can see why a raised liver test is baffling when you barely drink — but here’s the key thing: alcohol is only ONE cause. By far the commonest reason for exactly your pattern is fat in the liver driven by your metabolism — we call it non-alcoholic fatty liver. So ‘I barely drink’ doesn’t rule out a liver cause; it actually points us to this one. And I’m genuinely not sitting here thinking you’ve got a drink problem."

"Look at the bigger picture from your bloods: your weight’s carrying some around the middle, your blood pressure’s up a bit, your sugar’s in the pre-diabetes range, your triglycerides are high. Those all travel together — it’s called metabolic syndrome — and the liver is just showing it on a blood test. The liver is the messenger."

"Now, rather than just re-checking the number and hoping, I want to do this properly: a simple calculation and a specific blood test to estimate whether there’s any scarring in the liver, and an ultrasound scan. Importantly, the liver NUMBER doesn’t tell us how much scarring there is — so we check that directly rather than guess."

"Here’s the good news, and it’s real: this is common, it’s a warning rather than a disaster, and it’s largely reversible — with the SAME changes. Losing even a bit of weight melts fat out of the liver, brings your sugar and blood pressure down, and cuts your heart risk, all at once. You’d be treating five things with one plan."

"This isn’t about blame — it’s a really useful early heads-up. Let’s make a realistic plan: some weight loss, sort the blood pressure and keep an eye on the sugar, look at the cholesterol. I’ll help, not lecture. Done together, your liver test usually improves and so does everything else."

"So: I’ll do the scarring assessment and the scan, sort the metabolic side, and we’ll recheck. If the scarring test flagged anything, I’d involve the liver specialists — but most people at your stage do really well. Let’s book a proper follow-up. You came in wanting me to say it’s nothing; what it actually is, is a fixable warning that’s worth acting on."

f.learning: A mildly raised ALT (hepatocellular pattern) with central obesity, pre-diabetes and raised triglycerides, minimal alcohol and a negative viral/autoimmune/iron screen is non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD/MAFLD) — metabolic, not alcohol — so "I barely drink so it can’t be my liver" is the misconception to correct. The examinable clinical point is to assess FIBROSIS RISK (FIB-4 score per BSG/BASL 2018, ELF test per NICE NG49 with 10.51 or above indicating advanced fibrosis, ultrasound) rather than merely re-checking the ALT or reassuring — because the ALT level does NOT reflect fibrosis severity (advanced fibrosis can occur with near-normal ALT). NAFLD is a metabolic-syndrome and cardiovascular-risk marker, so manage the WHOLE picture (weight/lifestyle as the key, largely-reversible treatment, plus BP, glucose, lipids, CVD risk), refer to hepatology if significant fibrosis. The hidden agenda is defensiveness masking avoidance of the weight/lifestyle conversation and a fear of being judged or that "liver" means something sinister; reframe without blame ("a fixable warning, treating five things with one plan"), give honest proportionate reassurance balanced with proper fibrosis assessment, and follow up. NAFLD is common and often benign, but a subset progress to non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH), fibrosis and cirrhosis. The key is to assess FIBROSIS RISK (e.g. a FIB-4 score (BSG/BASL 2018), or an enhanced liver fibrosis/ELF test per NICE NG49, where ELF 10.51 or above indicates advanced fibrosis) rather than just reassure or re-check the ALT — and crucially, the ALT level does NOT reflect fibrosis severity (you can have advanced fibrosis with near-normal ALT).

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG49 (MASLD, formerly NAFLD; updated July 2026) · BSG/BASL abnormal liver blood tests guideline (Newsome et al., 2018) · NICE PH38 (type 2 diabetes: prevention in people at high risk, 2012) · NICE NG136 (hypertension, 2019) · NICE NG238 (cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, 2023) · NICE NG246 (overweight and obesity management, 2025)
knowledge.summary: A persistently raised ALT with central obesity, raised triglycerides, borderline BP and HbA1c in the high-risk range, minimal alcohol and a negative liver screen is fatty liver disease driven by metabolism (NAFLD, now also called MASLD). Assess fibrosis, not just the ALT, and treat the whole cardiometabolic picture without blame.

points.h: Why it’s his liver without the drink
points.t: Fatty liver disease linked to insulin resistance is a common cause of a mildly raised ALT in people with central obesity, dyslipidaemia, raised glucose or hypertension. By definition it occurs without significant alcohol intake. Other causes (viral hepatitis, iron overload, autoimmune disease, drugs, alcohol) are excluded by the liver aetiology screen (BSG/BASL 2018).

The ALT level does not reflect the degree of fibrosis; advanced fibrosis can exist with a normal or near-normal ALT. The prognostic question is fibrosis, so rechecking the ALT alone answers nothing (BSG/BASL 2018).

BSG/BASL 2018: use a non-invasive score such as FIB-4 (age, AST, ALT, platelets) first; a high score (above 3.25) indicates likely advanced fibrosis. NICE NG49: offer the ELF blood test to people with NAFLD; ELF 10.51 or above indicates advanced fibrosis — refer to a hepatologist. If below 10.51, NG49 suggests retesting adults every 3 years. Ultrasound shows fat but cannot stage fibrosis.

HbA1c 42–47 mmol/mol = high risk of type 2 diabetes: offer an intensive lifestyle programme and recheck at least yearly (NICE PH38). Clinic BP ≥140/90: offer ambulatory or home monitoring to confirm (NICE NG136). Calculate QRISK3 and offer atorvastatin 20 mg if ≥10% (NICE NG238).

NICE NG238: do not routinely exclude people from statin treatment because their liver transaminases are raised but less than 3 times the upper limit of normal. Cardiovascular disease is a leading cause of death in people with fatty liver, so a raised ALT is not a reason to withhold statins.

Weight loss through diet and activity reduces liver fat and improves the other risk factors together. Use NICE NG246 for a structured, non-judgemental weight-management conversation and local tier 2 services. Alcohol: advise keeping within the UK CMO low-risk guideline of no more than 14 units a week.

Fatty liver disease versus alcohol, drugs or supplements; negative viral, iron and autoimmune screen reviewed.
Asked about jaundice, itch, dark urine, ascites and abdominal pain; recognised that ALT does not exclude advanced fibrosis.

model.text: Hello Mr Hollis, I’m Dr Lee. Thanks for joining. I know the liver result has been on your mind — what did you make of it when you heard?
model.why: Opens with his interpretation of the result

model.text: Honestly, it baffled me. I barely drink — a couple of beers at the weekend. So it can’t be my liver, surely? Maybe it was a paracetamol I took. And I haven’t got a drink problem, if that’s what you’re thinking.
I’m not thinking that at all, and I’ll explain why in a moment. I’d like to check a couple of things with you, go through what the tests show, and agree a sensible plan. Does that work?
model.why: Defuses the defensiveness and sets a clear agenda

model.text: Fine. As long as you’re not going to lecture me.
No lectures, I promise. So I get it right — roughly how much do you drink in a typical week?
model.why: Confirms alcohol intake factually, without making it the focus

model.text: A couple of beers at the weekend. That’s it.
That’s well within the low-risk guideline, so alcohol isn’t the explanation here. How much paracetamol have you been taking, and any other tablets, supplements or herbal remedies?
Just the odd paracetamol for a headache. Nothing else.
That wouldn’t cause a rise that shows up twice. The bloods were for tiredness — how are you in yourself? Any yellowing of the eyes or skin, itching, dark urine, tummy swelling or pain?
model.why: Screens for symptoms of decompensated or other liver disease

model.text: None of that. Just tired. I’m an accountant — long days at a desk.
Tell me about a normal day for food and activity.
model.why: Open question into lifestyle without judgement

model.text: Not great, if I’m honest. Whatever’s quick when work’s busy, and not much exercise these days.
You mentioned wondering what I’d think. Is there a worry sitting behind this for you?
If I’m honest… ‘liver’ sounds serious. Cirrhosis, that kind of thing. I’d rather it was a blip and we move on.
That’s a very understandable worry, and I’m glad you said it. What were you hoping I’d say today?
model.why: Validates the fear and elicits his expectation

model.text: That it’s nothing.

Let me be straight with you, because I think the truth is more reassuring than ‘nothing’. Alcohol is only one cause of a raised liver test. The commonest cause in someone who barely drinks is fat building up in the liver, driven by metabolism. We call it fatty liver disease.
model.why: Corrects the misconception with a clear working diagnosis

model.text: Fat in the liver? From what?

Look at the rest of your results: carrying weight around the middle, blood pressure a little high, sugar in the range that means a higher risk of diabetes, and raised blood fats called triglycerides. Those travel together. The liver is just the one that showed up on a blood test — the messenger.
model.why: Links the liver result to the metabolic cluster

model.text: So it isn’t cirrhosis?

The other tests ruled out the viral and inherited causes, which is good. But I don’t want to guess about scarring, because the liver number doesn’t tell us how much scarring there is — people can have scarring with a near-normal result. So I’d like a specific blood test that estimates scarring directly. If that’s high, I’ll refer you to the liver specialists. Most people at this stage don’t have significant scarring.
model.why: Plans fibrosis assessment and explains why ALT is not enough

model.text: Okay. That’s fairer than just repeating the test.

Here’s the genuinely good news: at this stage, fatty liver is largely reversible. The same changes that take fat out of the liver also bring down your sugar, your blood pressure and your heart risk. One plan, several benefits.
model.why: Reframes as a fixable warning, which motivates without blame

model.text: Go on then. What would that look like?
You tell me what’s realistic. What’s one thing that would genuinely fit around your work?
model.why: Shared decision-making that respects his constraints

model.text: Probably the quick convenience food. And I could get out for a walk at lunchtime.

Both excellent. I’ll also refer you to the diabetes prevention programme — it’s free and built for exactly your blood results. And I’d like you to check your blood pressure at home for a week, because one clinic reading isn’t enough to decide anything.
model.why: Acts on the pre-diabetes and confirms BP per guidance

model.text: I’ll also work out your heart risk score. If it comes back 10% or more, I’d offer a cholesterol tablet — and a raised liver test like yours isn’t a reason to avoid one.
model.why: Addresses CVD risk and pre-empts a common statin misconception

model.text: I’d have assumed a statin was bad for the liver.
A common belief, but not at this level. So: scarring test, home blood pressure readings, heart risk score, the diabetes programme, and your two changes. Can you tell me back what you’ll do first?
model.why: Summarises and checks understanding with teach-back

model.text: Get the blood test done, borrow a BP monitor, cut the convenience food and walk at lunch.

Perfect. If you ever notice yellow eyes or skin, dark urine, swelling of your tummy or legs, vomiting blood or black stools, contact us the same day. Otherwise, I’ll see you in about four weeks with the scarring result and your readings, and we’ll recheck the liver and sugar tests in a few months. You came wanting to hear it was nothing — what it is, is a warning you’ve caught early.
model.why: Specific red flags, booked follow-up and a positive close

model.text: Fair enough. Thanks, doctor — that’s actually made me want to do something about it.

social.t: Long desk-bound days can drive convenience eating and inactivity. Plan changes around work rather than against it.
Many people equate liver disease with alcohol misuse. Addressing this directly lowers defensiveness and helps engagement.

legal.t: No DVLA notification or fitness-for-work issue arises from fatty liver at this stage.

professional.t: NICE NG246: discuss weight respectfully, with the person’s consent, and avoid stigmatising language. Offer referral to weight-management services where appropriate.
A repeated abnormal ALT needs a documented plan — fibrosis assessment and review — not a filed “repeat in 3 months”.

community.t: NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme; local tier 2 weight-management services; British Liver Trust for patient information; community pharmacy BP checks.

Abdominal swelling, leg swelling, confusion or bruising — possible decompensated liver disease
Unexplained weight loss or right upper quadrant mass

Work hours, eating pattern and activity

playbook.diagnosis: Probable metabolic fatty liver disease (NAFLD/MASLD) within a cardiometabolic cluster: “Your liver test is raised because fat has built up in the liver, linked to your weight, sugar, blood pressure and blood fats — not alcohol.”
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Think of the liver as a warning light on a car dashboard. It isn’t the engine failing — it’s telling us about the fuel system: weight, sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol. Fix those and the light usually goes off.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted to hear it was nothing, and you were worried about cirrhosis. The honest answer is in between — it’s something, it’s common, and it’s very fixable.”
management.psychosocial: Frame change around his working life: less convenience food and a lunchtime walk that he chose, supported by the diabetes prevention programme rather than a lecture.
sharedPlan: Fibrosis assessment: FIB-4 (BSG/BASL 2018) and ELF (NICE NG49); hepatology referral if ELF ≥10.51
Diabetes prevention programme and HbA1c recheck (NICE PH38); home or ambulatory BP (NICE NG136)
QRISK3; atorvastatin 20 mg if ≥10% (NICE NG238), not withheld for ALT below 3× ULN
safetyNet: Jaundice, dark urine, abdominal or leg swelling, vomiting blood or black stools: same-day contact
Review in about four weeks with results; recheck liver tests and HbA1c in a few months

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed less on hepatology than on two reflexes: reassuring a mildly raised ALT away, and implying the patient must be drinking. Both are common in examiner feedback and both are fixable.

items.fail: “It’s only mildly raised — let’s repeat it in three months.”
items.why: The ALT does not reflect fibrosis. Rechecking it without a fibrosis assessment misses the one finding that changes management (BSG/BASL 2018; NICE NG49).
items.fix: Arrange FIB-4 and/or ELF and explain why: “The liver number doesn’t show scarring, so I’ll check that directly.”

items.fail: Pressing him repeatedly on alcohol after he has given a clear, low intake.
items.why: It confirms the judgement he feared and damages Relating to Others. His intake is consistent with the diagnosis.
items.fix: Ask once, factually, then move on: “That’s within the low-risk guideline — this isn’t about alcohol.”

items.fail: Treating the liver as the whole problem and ignoring BP 142/90, HbA1c 44 and the triglycerides.
items.why: Fatty liver is a marker of cardiometabolic risk; missing the rest loses marks for managing comorbidity.
items.fix: Name the cluster and act on each part: home BP (NICE NG136), diabetes prevention (NICE PH38), QRISK3 (NICE NG238).

items.fail: Advising him to avoid statins because of his liver test.
items.why: NICE NG238 says not to routinely exclude people with transaminases raised but below 3 times the upper limit of normal.
items.fix: “A raised liver test at this level isn’t a reason to avoid a statin if your heart risk warrants one.”

items.fail: A long monologue on metabolic syndrome with jargon such as “steatosis” and “fibrosis markers”.
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient” is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Use plain images: “fat in the liver”, “a test for scarring”, “the liver as the messenger”.

items.fail: Ending with “lose some weight and we’ll see” and no agreed goals.
items.why: No shared plan and no check of understanding — marked down in both Relating and Tasks.
items.fix: Let him choose one or two changes, then teach-back: “What will you do first?”

SCA_MODELS.text: So it isn’t cirrhosis?

The other tests ruled out the viral and inherited causes, which is good. But I don’t want to guess about scarring, because the liver number doesn’t tell us how much scarring there is — people can have scarring with a near-normal result. So I’d like a specific blood test that estimates scarring directly. If that’s high, I’ll refer you to the liver specialists. Most people at this stage don’t have significant scarring.
SCA_MODELS.why: Plans fibrosis assessment and explains why ALT is not enough

SCA_MODELS.text: Okay. That’s fairer than just repeating the test.

Here’s the genuinely good news: at this stage, fatty liver is largely reversible. The same changes that take fat out of the liver also bring down your sugar, your blood pressure and your heart risk. One plan, several benefits.
SCA_MODELS.why: Reframes as a fixable warning, which motivates without blame

SCA_MODELS.text: Go on then. What would that look like?
You tell me what’s realistic. What’s one thing that would genuinely fit around your work?
SCA_MODELS.why: Shared decision-making that respects his constraints

SCA_MODELS.text: Probably the quick convenience food. And I could get out for a walk at lunchtime.

Both excellent. I’ll also refer you to the diabetes prevention programme — it’s free and built for exactly your blood results. And I’d like you to check your blood pressure at home for a week, because one clinic reading isn’t enough to decide anything.
SCA_MODELS.why: Acts on the pre-diabetes and confirms BP per guidance

SCA_MODELS.text: I’ll also work out your heart risk score. If it comes back 10% or more, I’d offer a cholesterol tablet — and a raised liver test like yours isn’t a reason to avoid one.
SCA_MODELS.why: Addresses CVD risk and pre-empts a common statin misconception

SCA_MODELS.text: I’d have assumed a statin was bad for the liver.
A common belief, but not at this level. So: scarring test, home blood pressure readings, heart risk score, the diabetes programme, and your two changes. Can you tell me back what you’ll do first?
SCA_MODELS.why: Summarises and checks understanding with teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: Get the blood test done, borrow a BP monitor, cut the convenience food and walk at lunch.

Perfect. If you ever notice yellow eyes or skin, dark urine, swelling of your tummy or legs, vomiting blood or black stools, contact us the same day. Otherwise, I’ll see you in about four weeks with the scarring result and your readings, and we’ll recheck the liver and sugar tests in a few months. You came wanting to hear it was nothing — what it is, is a warning you’ve caught early.
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific red flags, booked follow-up and a positive close

SCA_MODELS.text: Fair enough. Thanks, doctor — that’s actually made me want to do something about it.

SCA_STEM.name: Gary Hollis
SCA_STEM.recent: Bloods for tiredness: ALT about 80 IU/L, raised again on repeat. Bilirubin, ALP and INR normal. Triglycerides raised. Hepatitis B and C negative; ferritin and autoimmune screen unremarkable. Alcohol: a few units a week.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video appointment to discuss his liver blood test. Works as an accountant.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: NICE NG49 (MASLD, formerly NAFLD; updated July 2026) · BSG/BASL abnormal liver blood tests guideline (Newsome et al., 2018) · NICE PH38 (type 2 diabetes: prevention in people at high risk, 2012) · NICE NG136 (hypertension, 2019) · NICE NG238 (cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, 2023) · NICE NG246 (overweight and obesity management, 2025)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A persistently raised ALT with central obesity, raised triglycerides, borderline BP and HbA1c in the high-risk range, minimal alcohol and a negative liver screen is fatty liver disease driven by metabolism (NAFLD, now also called MASLD). Assess fibrosis, not just the ALT, and treat the whole cardiometabolic picture without blame.

points.h: Why it’s his liver without the drink
points.t: Fatty liver disease linked to insulin resistance is a common cause of a mildly raised ALT in people with central obesity, dyslipidaemia, raised glucose or hypertension. By definition it occurs without significant alcohol intake. Other causes (viral hepatitis, iron overload, autoimmune disease, drugs, alcohol) are excluded by the liver aetiology screen (BSG/BASL 2018).

The ALT level does not reflect the degree of fibrosis; advanced fibrosis can exist with a normal or near-normal ALT. The prognostic question is fibrosis, so rechecking the ALT alone answers nothing (BSG/BASL 2018).

BSG/BASL 2018: use a non-invasive score such as FIB-4 (age, AST, ALT, platelets) first; a high score (above 3.25) indicates likely advanced fibrosis. NICE NG49: offer the ELF blood test to people with NAFLD; ELF 10.51 or above indicates advanced fibrosis — refer to a hepatologist. If below 10.51, NG49 suggests retesting adults every 3 years. Ultrasound shows fat but cannot stage fibrosis.

HbA1c 42–47 mmol/mol = high risk of type 2 diabetes: offer an intensive lifestyle programme and recheck at least yearly (NICE PH38). Clinic BP ≥140/90: offer ambulatory or home monitoring to confirm (NICE NG136). Calculate QRISK3 and offer atorvastatin 20 mg if ≥10% (NICE NG238).

NICE NG238: do not routinely exclude people from statin treatment because their liver transaminases are raised but less than 3 times the upper limit of normal. Cardiovascular disease is a leading cause of death in people with fatty liver, so a raised ALT is not a reason to withhold statins.

Weight loss through diet and activity reduces liver fat and improves the other risk factors together. Use NICE NG246 for a structured, non-judgemental weight-management conversation and local tier 2 services. Alcohol: advise keeping within the UK CMO low-risk guideline of no more than 14 units a week.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Asked what he made of the result, and let him voice “I barely drink” without argument.
Work pattern, desk-based job, eating habits, activity, and his defensiveness about alcohol.
Picked up “I haven’t got a drink problem” and “I’d rather it was a blip”, and explored the fear of cirrhosis.
Idea (alcohol is the only liver cause), concern (serious liver disease, being judged), expectation (told it’s nothing).
Fibrosis assessment (FIB-4 per BSG/BASL 2018 and ELF per NICE NG49), home or ambulatory BP, QRISK3, repeat HbA1c; abdominal examination and ultrasound as locally indicated.
Fatty liver disease versus alcohol, drugs or supplements; negative viral, iron and autoimmune screen reviewed.
Asked about jaundice, itch, dark urine, ascites and abdominal pain; recognised that ALT does not exclude advanced fibrosis.
Named metabolic fatty liver disease within a cardiometabolic cluster, in plain words.
Fibrosis test with hepatology referral if ELF ≥10.51 (NICE NG49); negotiated lifestyle goals; diabetes prevention programme (NICE PH38).
Confirmed BP out of clinic (NICE NG136); QRISK3 with statin offer if ≥10%, not withheld for ALT <3× ULN (NICE NG238).
Review in about four weeks; recheck liver tests and HbA1c; same-day contact for jaundice, ascites, GI bleeding.

social.t: Long desk-bound days can drive convenience eating and inactivity. Plan changes around work rather than against it.
Many people equate liver disease with alcohol misuse. Addressing this directly lowers defensiveness and helps engagement.

legal.t: No DVLA notification or fitness-for-work issue arises from fatty liver at this stage.

professional.t: NICE NG246: discuss weight respectfully, with the person’s consent, and avoid stigmatising language. Offer referral to weight-management services where appropriate.
A repeated abnormal ALT needs a documented plan — fibrosis assessment and review — not a filed “repeat in 3 months”.

community.t: NHS Diabetes Prevention Programme; local tier 2 weight-management services; British Liver Trust for patient information; community pharmacy BP checks.

redFlags: Jaundice, dark urine, pale stools or itch
Abdominal swelling, leg swelling, confusion or bruising — possible decompensated liver disease
Unexplained weight loss or right upper quadrant mass
psychosocial: Alcohol units stated plainly, then moved on from
Work hours, eating pattern and activity
Fear of cirrhosis and of being judged as a drinker
ice: Idea: “I barely drink, so it can’t be my liver — probably a blip or a paracetamol”
Concern: that “liver” means something serious, and being judged
Expectation: reassurance that it’s nothing and to move on

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Probable metabolic fatty liver disease (NAFLD/MASLD) within a cardiometabolic cluster: “Your liver test is raised because fat has built up in the liver, linked to your weight, sugar, blood pressure and blood fats — not alcohol.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Think of the liver as a warning light on a car dashboard. It isn’t the engine failing — it’s telling us about the fuel system: weight, sugar, blood pressure and cholesterol. Fix those and the light usually goes off.”

management.reflectIce: “You wanted to hear it was nothing, and you were worried about cirrhosis. The honest answer is in between — it’s something, it’s common, and it’s very fixable.”
management.psychosocial: Frame change around his working life: less convenience food and a lunchtime walk that he chose, supported by the diabetes prevention programme rather than a lecture.
sharedPlan: Fibrosis assessment: FIB-4 (BSG/BASL 2018) and ELF (NICE NG49); hepatology referral if ELF ≥10.51
Diabetes prevention programme and HbA1c recheck (NICE PH38); home or ambulatory BP (NICE NG136)
QRISK3; atorvastatin 20 mg if ≥10% (NICE NG238), not withheld for ALT below 3× ULN
safetyNet: Jaundice, dark urine, abdominal or leg swelling, vomiting blood or black stools: same-day contact
Review in about four weeks with results; recheck liver tests and HbA1c in a few months

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed less on hepatology than on two reflexes: reassuring a mildly raised ALT away, and implying the patient must be drinking. Both are common in examiner feedback and both are fixable.

items.fail: “It’s only mildly raised — let’s repeat it in three months.”
items.why: The ALT does not reflect fibrosis. Rechecking it without a fibrosis assessment misses the one finding that changes management (BSG/BASL 2018; NICE NG49).
items.fix: Arrange FIB-4 and/or ELF and explain why: “The liver number doesn’t show scarring, so I’ll check that directly.”

items.fail: Pressing him repeatedly on alcohol after he has given a clear, low intake.
items.why: It confirms the judgement he feared and damages Relating to Others. His intake is consistent with the diagnosis.
items.fix: Ask once, factually, then move on: “That’s within the low-risk guideline — this isn’t about alcohol.”

items.fail: Treating the liver as the whole problem and ignoring BP 142/90, HbA1c 44 and the triglycerides.
items.why: Fatty liver is a marker of cardiometabolic risk; missing the rest loses marks for managing comorbidity.
items.fix: Name the cluster and act on each part: home BP (NICE NG136), diabetes prevention (NICE PH38), QRISK3 (NICE NG238).

items.fail: Advising him to avoid statins because of his liver test.
items.why: NICE NG238 says not to routinely exclude people with transaminases raised but below 3 times the upper limit of normal.
items.fix: “A raised liver test at this level isn’t a reason to avoid a statin if your heart risk warrants one.”

items.fail: A long monologue on metabolic syndrome with jargon such as “steatosis” and “fibrosis markers”.
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient” is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Use plain images: “fat in the liver”, “a test for scarring”, “the liver as the messenger”.

items.fail: Ending with “lose some weight and we’ll see” and no agreed goals.
items.why: No shared plan and no check of understanding — marked down in both Relating and Tasks.
items.fix: Let him choose one or two changes, then teach-back: “What will you do first?”
